items.title: Dozens of inquests reveal mental health care failures in NSW prisons (ABC, 31 October 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Kirstie Wellauer, Joanna McCarthy, Josh Nicholas and Katia Shatoba, ABC News, 31 October 2026 — an ABC review of NSW coronial findings, January 2015 to September 2026; Coroners Act 2009 (NSW) ss 22, 23, 78, 81, 82; Premier's Memorandum M2009-12
items.significance: The ABC found mental health care failures in 48 of 249 NSW prison inquests — and Corrections did not fully support recommendations in 10 of 32, because coroners can recommend but not compel.
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - NSW Prison Inquests Mental Health Failures Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
The ABC reviewed **249** coronial inquests into NSW prison deaths since 2015. **48** found failures in mental health
care — screening (20), supervision (14), clinical care (27), waits for care (29); **14** of those 48 deaths involved
Indigenous people. Corrections did not fully support recommendations in **10 of 32** inquests. The story centres on
**Bailey Mackander**, who died in November 2019; after the 2021 inquest, Corrections refused five recommendations on
risk intervention team cells.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.8 (post-sentencing)** — conditions and care in custody; most people in custody are on remand.
- **crime.3.1** — the Coroners Court's role and its limits.
- **Effectiveness** — accountability that depends on agencies choosing to act.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of an ABC data investigation**; failure categories overlap. Treat Bailey's family's story
with care.

sections.What a coroner can and cannot do:
| Can | Cannot |
|---|---|
| Hold a **mandatory inquest** into a death in custody, led by a senior coroner (s 22(2)) | Find guilt — findings must not suggest an offence (s 81(3)) |
| Record identity, date, place, manner and cause of death (s 81(1)) | Prosecute — only refer papers to the DPP (s 78) |
| Make recommendations to prevent similar deaths (s 82) | **Compel** an agency to act |
| Expect a response within six months (M2009-12) | Enforce that deadline — the memorandum is not mandatory |

The RCIADIC asked for responses within **three** months; NSW chose six. A 2023 statutory review (Rec 40) proposed
legislating the response duty and publishing responses on the Coroners Court website.

items.title: Post-Bondi policing bill soars as the Armed Response Command replaces Operation Shelter (SMH, 2 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Clair Weaver and Riley Walter, The Sydney Morning Herald, 2 November 2026, reporting NSW Police Operation Shelter costs obtained under freedom of information; LEPRA 2002 (NSW) s 230; Law Enforcement Conduct Commission Act 2016 (NSW) ss 44, 110, 113 and Part 8
items.significance: A surge operation after the 7 October 2023 attack cost $41.8m in 2025/26 and is becoming a permanent rifle-armed command of 250 officers — with no rules on where it operates, protests included.
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - Operation Shelter Armed Response Command Costs Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Operation Shelter** began in October 2023 to police tension after the 7 October attack on Israel, rotating
officers from local commands. FOI documents show its annual cost rose from **$4.1m** in its first year to **$41.8m**
in 2025/26, and **$53.7m** in the ten months after the 14 December 2025 Bondi attack. The **Armed Response Command**
(ARC), announced in February 2026, became operational on **1 November 2026** at an establishment cost of **$94.3m**.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.2.1** — police powers and resourcing reshaped by a terror attack; accountability for force.
- **crime.1.9** — situational prevention and visible deterrence at a high cost.
- **Balance** — community safety against peaceful protest.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of an FOI-based report** supplied by the teacher (subscriber article); the FOI documents
are unpublished. Only the Minister and a supportive envoy are quoted.

sections.Operation Shelter v the ARC:
| | Operation Shelter (2023–) | Armed Response Command (2026–) |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Surge operation, officers rotated from local commands | Permanent 24/7 command with an operations centre |
| Staffing | About 97% of cost is shifts, overtime and allowances | **250** officers and 28 civilian staff |
| Weapons | General duties officers with pistols (e.g. Chanukah 2025) | Australian Combat Assault Rifles; 24 vehicles with gun safes |
| Cost | $41.8m (2025/26) | $94.3m to set up; operating budget "absorbed" |
| Protests | Remit included large protests | No rules restricting where it operates; protests not ruled out |
sections.How armed force is checked:
LEPRA **s 230**: force reasonably necessary → if death or serious injury, a **critical incident** (LECC Act s 110) →
police investigate themselves (s 113; often 2–3 years) → the **LECC** monitors but cannot investigate the officers
until police finish (s 44(9)) → final advice and recommendations. Amnesty seeks independent oversight of the ARC.

items.title: Younger offenders and online recruitment — headlines v the data (SMH, 1 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Ben Cubby, The Sydney Morning Herald, 1 November 2026, set against BOCSAR youth crime and custody data to June 2026; Bail Act 2013 (NSW) s 22C; Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) s 5; Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)
items.significance: Despite talk of a youth crime 'tsunami', youth court proceedings are stable and down 8% over 15 years — yet youth detention rose 34% in two years, mostly remand under stricter bail laws.
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - Youth Crime Younger Offenders Online Recruitment Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
Police and the AFP warn of younger children involved in violent crime and recruited online by organised crime.
BOCSAR data says otherwise about volume: young people proceeded against to court are **down 8%** over 15 years and
stable over two. But detention rose **34%** (June 2023 to June 2025), and in March 2026 **175 of 220** (79.6%) young
people in detention were **on remand**, not sentenced. Proven outcomes for 10–13-year-olds fell from **76% to 16%**
(2015–16 to 2022–23).
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.5.1 / crime.1.8** — age of criminal responsibility, causes of youth offending, and media framing.
- **Effectiveness** — whether bail tightening, not crime, drives detention.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of a subscriber feature** supplied by the teacher; some figures and legal details in the
article are simplified or misdated (flagged in the summary).

sections.Headlines v the data:
| Claim | What the sources show |
|---|---|
| AFP: a "tsunami of youth crime" | Given to a radicalisation inquiry; about extremism and sadistic online networks |
| 34% detention jump since bail rules began "April last year" | 34% is June 2023–June 2025; s 22C began April 2024 |
| Bail law covers any prior property charge | Only motor theft or serious break and enter, allegedly while on bail for one |
| School attendance the strongest predictor | By 15, suspension data dominates |
| Scotland has no child prisoners | No under-18s in young offender institutions; secure care still used |

**doli incapax** for 10–13-year-olds (prosecution must prove the child knew the act was seriously wrong; s 5 from 1
March 2026) → Children's Court (in 2022–23, 53% of 10–13-year-olds had all charges withdrawn).

items.title: Secretary, Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water v Dalton [2026] NSWLEC 138
items.citation: [2026] NSWLEC 138
items.significance: A landholder who cleared 944.9 ha of native vegetation was fined $90,000 and $135,000 after a 25% plea discount, so that illegal clearing no longer pays.
core_labels: Types of crime — strict liability, summary and indictable, crimes against people and property
items.document: Cases/Crime/Secretary DCCEEW v Dalton [2026] NSWLEC 138 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Secretary DCCEEW v Dalton [2026] NSWLEC 138 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
A landholder pleaded guilty at the first opportunity to two counts of clearing native vegetation in a
regulated rural area (s 60N, *Local Land Services Act 2013* (NSW)), about 545.6 ha in May–June 2023 and
399.3 ha in September–October 2023, far beyond what he had notified. He also admitted a Form 1 offence
of knowingly damaging the habitat of a threatened species (s 2.4, *Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016*).
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.3 and crime.4.6** — factors in sentencing, and a fines-only outcome with ancillary orders.
- **dis.1.3** — s 60N is a strict-liability regulatory offence, yet planning still raises seriousness.
- **Compliance and effectiveness** — can a fine be large enough to deter a profit-driven offence?
items.caution:
The judgment's area figures conflict (944.9 ha is the offence total). The offender's means to pay are
not in the file. The Form 1 offence is taken into account, not punished separately.

sections.Held — Pritchard J:
- The harm was **of some seriousness but not substantial**, so the s 21A(2)(g) aggravating factor was
  not engaged; no practical measures were taken and he had complete control.
- The offending was **planned and for financial gain**; the s 60N offences were at the lower end of
  moderate objective seriousness.
- A 25% discount for the early plea took $120,000 and $180,000 to **$90,000 and $135,000**.
  Half of each fine goes to the prosecutor, he pays costs, and notices are published in four newspapers.
- General deterrence requires penalties that make "the financial cost ... of clearing native vegetation
  illegally outweigh the commercial gain".

items.title: WA Police scan 1.38 million faces in a live facial recognition trial (The Guardian, 2 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Ima Caldwell and Penry Buckley, The Guardian Australia, 2 November 2026, on the WA Police overt live facial recognition trial; read with the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) ss 4, 27, the Privacy and Responsible Information Sharing Act 2024 (WA) and the WA Police privacy impact assessment (v1.0, May 2026)
items.significance: A five-month WA police trial scanned 1.38 million faces for 122 arrests and nine false alerts, with no specific statute, no individual suspicion and the privacy watchdog on the sidelines.
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - WA Police Facial Recognition Trial Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead: In a trial that ended on **31 October 2026**, WA Police scanned **1,380,882** faces from marked vans over **100 deployments at 43 locations** (including three operations at the Perth royal show) and matched them against a police alert list. The result: **122 arrests**, **146** engagements with registered sex offenders, **10** welfare checks and **nine incorrect alerts**. Vans are off the road while police run an internal evaluation.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.2.1 Police powers** and **crime.2.3 Investigating crime**: mass biometric scanning with no individual suspicion, against the reasonable-suspicion threshold that governs other police powers.
- **Balancing victims, suspects and society** (the question asked in HSC 2014 Q24): alerts on registered sex offenders and 122 arrests against false matches, bias and privacy. The summary's exemplar paragraph answers that question.
- **Beyond Crime**: Human Rights hr.3.1 (privacy and technology as a contemporary issue); Year 11 notes on the individual and technology.
items.caution: A news report of **police-supplied, unaudited figures**, not the evaluation, which is pending. It was read from a saved copy because the Guardian page could not be fetched. Western Australian, not NSW, law. Not confirmed: the Australian Human Rights Commission's 2021 report on facial recognition (date and wording) and the arrest threshold in s 128 of the Criminal Investigation Act. Check the police evaluation before relying on the figures.

sections.The claims and the checks:
| Claim | What the checking found |
|---|---|
| Error rate was **0.00065%** | The arithmetic is right (9 ÷ 1,380,882) but it divides false alerts by *scans*, not by *alerts*. At the three-month update 8 of 209 alerts (about 3.8%) were wrong. The final number of alerts is not published |
| Non-matches are pixelated and deleted at once | A police claim. The privacy impact assessment says non-matching data is deleted at once but does not mention pixelation. No independent audit was found |
| Scans were done "with no reasonable suspicion" (Civil Liberties Australia) | The scans are indiscriminate and the assessment names no specific statutory power. Reasonable suspicion (s 4, *Criminal Investiga…
sections.The legal frame:
- **No specific statute** authorises the scans. WA Police rely on the *Privacy and Responsible Information Sharing Act 2024* (WA), which commenced on 1 July 2026, after the trial began; the Information Commissioner (OIC WA) said it was not part of the design and warned of "collective privacy harms".
- The Commonwealth *Privacy Act 1988* does not cover State police. When Human Rights Watch last wrote (2021) WA had no human rights act; its status in November 2026 was not checked.
- Comparators: the OAIC's *Clearview AI* determination (2021), *Bridges v South Wales Police* (UK Court of Appeal, 2020) and the EU AI Act's limits on real-time police biometric identification.

items.title: Zakaria seeks permanent stay over alleged unlawful deportation — the Crown concession and suppressed AFP evidence (2026)
items.citation: HSC Legal Studies evidence summaries, 19, 21 and 26 October and 2 and 3 November 2026; built on ABC News of 18, 19, 22, 24 and 31 October 2026 with its earlier reports of September 2025 and July 2026, AAP, the AFP's December 2023 release, Moti v The Queen [2011] HCA 50 and the abuse-of-process authorities

items.document: Crime/Criminal Trial Process/Zakaria permanent stay - AFP removal on trial (Evidence summary 3Nov26).pdf
items.lead:
Masood Zakaria, 31, charged over the **20 October 2021** Guildford murders of Salim and Toufik
Hamze, asks the Supreme Court to **permanently stay** his prosecution as an abuse of process, arguing
the AFP's role in his return from Türkiye was unlawful. The hearing opened before **Justice Edward
Muston on 19 October 2026**. **Everything here is an allegation; nothing has been tested at trial,
and the stay has not been decided.**
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.3.1 / crime.3.6 (court jurisdiction, pre-trial process)** — a pre-trial application doing
  real work, and the court's own integrity as a legal interest distinct from guilt.
- **crime.2.1 / crime.6.2 (police powers, international cooperation)** — police acting outside formal

items.title: House prices fall a seventh month as investor tax changes bite (ABC, 2 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Nassim Khadem, ABC News, 2 November 2026, reporting Cotality's October 2026 Home Value Index; Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026 (Cth); draft Tax Reform No. 3 Bill 2026
items.significance: The first big test of tax law as a housing affordability tool: after negative gearing and CGT concessions were cut, national values fell 1.2% in October, 6.7% below the March peak — while rents rose 5.5%.
items.document: Shelter/Evidence Sheets/Shelter - House Prices Seventh Fall and Investor Tax Changes Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
National home values fell **1.2%** in October 2026, a **seventh** monthly fall, leaving them **6.7%** (about $63,400) below
the March peak; sales were **23%** lower over three months than a year earlier. The national median weekly rent is
**$713**, up 5.5% over the year. Higher interest rates (four RBA rises) and the tax changes both contributed; the
article does not separate them.
items.use_it_for:
- **shel.1.4 / shel.3.1** — federal tax law as a shelter policy lever; gains for buyers against risks for renters and
  supply.
- **Law reform** — budget → legislation → market response.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of a market news report** drawing on industry data and agents; no government, renter or
advocate voice.

sections.What changes for investors (from 1 July:
| | Now | After 1 July 2027 |
|---|---|---|
| Negative gearing | Rental losses on any property deductible against wages | Only for **new builds**; established-home losses offset property income only |
| Grandfathering | — | Properties held before 7:30pm AEST, 12 May 2026, exempt |
| CGT | 50% discount after a year | **Inflation indexation** on gains accruing from 1 July 2027 |

items.significance: NCAT refused a late adjournment and appointed the Public Guardian for three years for an older woman with dementia, with last-resort conditions on restrictive practices.

items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Kathy (a pseudonym) (No 2) [2026] NSWCATGD 21 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
A carer sought an adjournment the night before a guardianship hearing, with no medical certificate and
after ignoring directions. The Tribunal proceeded. All names are pseudonyms.

sections.Held — the Tribunal (decision 18 August:
- Adjournment refused: Kathy's welfare is the paramount concern (s 4, *Guardianship Act 1987*), and the carer
  "has been afforded opportunities to present her case ... though has not availed herself".
- Kathy needed a guardian: Alzheimer's dementia leaves her partly incapable of managing her person.
- The **Public Guardian** was appointed for three years because no suitable private person was proposed
  (s 15(3)), with functions including accommodation, health care and consent to restrictive practices
  only as a last resort and under a behaviour support plan.

items.title: Lee and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2513
items.significance: An extension of time to review a citizenship refusal was refused: 347 days late, notice went to the email she nominated, and she could reapply.
core_labels: Addressing disputes through government reviews, courts and tribunals
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Lee and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] ARTA 2513 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
A delegate refused an application for Australian citizenship (s 21(4)(e), *Australian Citizenship Act 2007*)
in June 2025 and sent the decision to the email address the applicant had nominated. She asked the
Tribunal for an extension of time on 15 June 2026, 347 days after the review period ended.
items.use_it_for: - **dis.3.4** — a government decision reviewed by a tribunal, and the time limit stage.
items.caution:
Year 11 only; no HSC link. The decision date is 3 or 4 June 2025 in the file. Paragraph numbers restart,
so quotes are unnumbered. The member and tribunal number are not in the file.

sections.Held — the Tribunal:
- Section 19 of the *Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024* allows an extension if "reasonable in all
  the circumstances", applying the *Hunter Valley Developments v Cohen* factors.
- The delay was extreme and unexplained; she "bore the responsibility of updating her contact details".
- The merits were weak on an impressionistic view; no prejudice was not enough; she could reapply.
- The application for an extension of time was refused.

items.title: NSW firearms reforms after Bondi and the National Gun Buyback (2025–2027)
items.citation: Terrorism and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2025 (NSW) (passed 24 December 2025); National Gun Buyback, NSW Government media release, 26 October 2026, and joint Commonwealth–NSW release, 16 August 2026
items.significance: After the 14 December 2025 Bondi Beach terror attack, NSW capped gun numbers, cut licences to two years and removed NCAT review, then opened a buyback for up to 274,000 firearms.
core_labels: Overview of the area of law reform
Executive methods — political will, parliamentary debate, ministerial directions
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - NSW Gun Buyback and Firearm Caps Evidence Summary.pdf
items.document11: Preliminary/Year 11 - National Gun Buyback Law Reform After Bondi Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
The **Bondi Beach terrorist attack** on 14 December 2025 killed 15 people. Ten days later NSW passed the
**Terrorism and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2025**, and in August 2026 NSW became the first state to
join a **National Gun Buyback**, citing recommendations 13 and 14 of a Royal Commission interim report.
Bookings opened on 26 October 2026; surrenders run from **2 November 2026** at six police stations,
widening in stages to February 2027, for about 12 months.

  opinion as drivers; **legislative** (the 2025 Act) and **executive** (the scheme) methods.
- **chg.4.1 / chg.4.2** — fewer guns against fixed compensation (one farmer paid $2,900 for a gun worth
  $850 under the schedule), uneven national uptake (Queensland, Victoria and the NT declined) and
  divided research on the 1996 Port Arthur buyback.
- **inv.5.2** — a state law with a Commonwealth-funded scheme: division of powers and cooperation.

sections.Before and after:
| | Before | After the 2025 Act |
|---|---|---|
| Number of guns | No fixed cap | **4** (recreational hunting, vermin) or **10** (most other genuine reasons); collectors and dealers unlimited |
| Licence term | Up to 5 years | **2 years** (licences from 1 July 2026) |
| Review of decisions | External appeal to **NCAT** | Internal review only (except Firearm Prohibition Orders) |
| Permit to acquire | — | Safe-storage inspection and terrorism-related checks first |
| Categories | Straight-pull, pump, lever-release lower | Moved to Category C; belt-fed prohibited |
| Club membership | Not required for all A/B holders | Required once proclaimed |

through in **three days** after Bondi. The Premier expects the demand-driven scheme to cost "hundreds of millions";
